t: Largest Triangle Area — Brute Force with the Shoelace Formula
o: We must pick any 3 of the given points and return the maximum triangle area they form. Since a triangle's area from three vertices is fully determined by the shoelace (cross-product) formula, the task reduces to evaluating all triples. In Example 1, checking all C(5,3)=10 triples gives the largest area 2.0 from points (0,0),(2,0),(0,2); in Example 2 there is only one triple, giving area 0.5. With n ≤ 50, there are at most C(50,3) = 19,600 triples, so an O(n^3) brute force is trivially fast — no clever geometry needed.
k: The area of a triangle with vertices (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3) equals |(x2-x1)(y3-y1) - (x3-x1)(y2-y1)| / 2 (shoelace / cross product).
With n ≤ 50, enumerating all O(n^3) triples (~20k) is fast enough; no optimization is required.
Take absolute value before halving so orientation of the three points doesn't matter.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over all triples
a.i: Try every combination of three distinct points and compute its area with the shoelace formula: area = |x1(y2-y3) + x2(y3-y1) + x3(y1-y2)| / 2. Track the maximum seen. Correctness follows because the answer is by definition the max over all triples, and we check each one exactly once.
s: Loop over all indices i < j < k.
Compute area = abs(x1*(y2-y3) + x2*(y3-y1) + x3*(y1-y2)) / 2 for points i, j, k.
a.t: O(n^3) — we examine all C(n,3) triples, at most ~19,600 for n=50.
a.sp: O(1) — only scalar variables are used beyond the input.

a.n: Approach 2: Cross product via vector subtraction (same complexity, cleaner math)
a.i: Instead of the expanded shoelace form, treat two edges as vectors u = B - A and v = C - A; the triangle area is |u × v| / 2 where the 2D cross product is ux*vy - uy*vx. This is numerically identical but often easier to derive and less error-prone to write under pressure.
s: For each ordered triple (A, B, C), form vectors u = B - A and v = C - A.
Compute cross = u.x * v.y - u.y * v.x.
a.t: O(n^3) — same enumeration of all triples as Approach 1.
a.sp: O(1) extra space (O(1) even counting Python's combinations iterator).

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 immediately: state the shoelace formula, note n ≤ 50 makes O(n^3) fine, and code it cleanly. Pitfalls: forgetting the absolute value (collinear or clockwise-ordered triples give negative signed area), dividing by 2 only after taking abs, and integer overflow in Java/C++ if using int for products (use long/double — coordinates up to 50 keep values small, but casting is safe practice). Edge cases: exactly 3 points, collinear points yielding area 0 (still valid input since answer tolerance handles it). Follow-ups might ask for faster methods for large n — mention that the optimal triangle's vertices lie on the convex hull, so you could hull first (O(n log n)) then brute-force the hull points, though worst case remains cubic when all points are on the hull.
